newsitem.title: USA: Divided U.S. panel releases Social Security report.
newsitem.headline: Divided U.S. panel releases Social Security report.

text.p: A deeply divided advisory panel Monday issued conflicting plans for protecting the long-term solvency of Social Security, though agreeing that some of the program's billions of dollars in payroll taxes should be invested in private markets.
The 13-member advisory group was appointed in 1994 to devise strategies for ensuring the future health of Social Security, which provides benefits to 44 million Americans.

The council split into three factions and while agreeing on a series of smaller changes that could address half of the long-term funding problems facing the program, was never able to agree on one plan to ensure its long-term solvency.
One faction, calls for radial privatization that would turn Social Security into a two-tiered benefit system. Under this option all retirees would receive a basic, flat benefit when they retire.

In addition, individuals would be set up personal savings account, similar to an individual retirement account (IRA). As much as five percentage points of the annual Social Security payroll tax would be invested in the accounts.
The transition to the new system would be funded by a 1.5 percent payroll tax or its equivalent.

A second group of six members, including labor union officials and former Social Security Commissioner Robert Ball, wants to preserve the current benefits structure with few changes while changing the way the government invests social security trust funds. This group suggests that the government, not individuals, might invest up to 40 percent of trust funds in private financial markets.

Currently, Social Security funds can be invested only in special issue treasury securities, which provide a low-risk but lower rate of return than other investments. Estimates are that shifting into market-based funds could increase the program's rate of return to 4.7 percent from the current 2.3 percent.
But there are divisions in this group, with Ball saying the government should move fast and others calling for further study.
A third option would add individual investment accounts to the system, financed by a new, mandatory contribution of 1.6 percent of payroll.

"The more radical of the proposals to dismantle Social Security would basically make the securities industry reponsible for administering America's basic retirement security," Ball told a news conference. "There is simply no compelling argument for abandoning the traditional Social Security program.
Illustrating bitter divisions, labor representatives have pledged to fight to kill any plan to allow individual investment, charging it would erode the system.
